claim.why_it_matters: The page-layout figure's three columns are flattened and interleaved: the form-position labels are fused with the PAGE clause phrase names ('Logical Top Heading', 'Logical Page Limit'), a two-row table splits 'Logical Top of Form' across rows, and the phrase names run into their content text, so a reader cannot tell which report content belongs to which PAGE phrase or form position. Informative annex E figure; no text is lost but the column association is.

verdict.reasoning: Checked against the 300 dpi render of PDF page 808 (printed page 786). Every label and content line of Figure E.8 is present in the markdown, in the printed order: Physical Top of Form / the first line that can be printed / <blank>; Logical Top of Form + Heading + the first line of the report or page heading / <(first page only) report header lines> / <page heading lines>; First Detail + the first line of a body group and the Control Heading/Detail/Control Footing stacks; Last Control Heading, Last Detail, Footing (including the PDF's own unclosed '<page footing lines.'), <(last page only) report footing lines>; Logical Bottom of Form + Page Limit + the last line on a logical page; Physical Bottom of Form + the last line that can be printed. The markdown reads each printed row left to right, so 'Logical Top Heading' and 'Logical Page Limit' are exactly what sits on one printed line (the italic form label's first line beside the bold phrase name), and 'of Form' falls on the line of '<(first page only) report header lines>' as it does in print. Each phrase name stays directly followed by its own content text, so the phrase-to-content association is recoverable; only the column alignment of an informative Annex E drawing is lost. The claim itself concedes no text is lost. That is layout/formatting of an informative figure, with no change of content or meaning, so it is not a genuine content discrepancy.
